source.title: Provable Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Benign Overfitting

record.tranche_reason: The paper theoretically analyzes weak-to-strong training and reports simulations of its effect on test generalization, but uses a stylized Gaussian-feature linear-classifier setup and test error/accuracy rather than Burns et al.'s pretrained-model benchmarks and PGR measure.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theorems and simulations bear on weak-to-strong generalization. Burns et al.'s empirical findings are cited background only and are not recorded as results. The PCA discussion and the correlated-Gaussian concentration result do not measure weak-to-strong behavior.
record.test_reason: The paper proves when a strong student trained on a weak teacher's hard pseudolabels generalizes or falls to chance, and runs finite-sample simulations. The setting is minimum-norm interpolating linear classifiers on Gaussian spiked-covariance features, not pretrained LMs, and it reports test error/accuracy rather than PGR. Its own theorems and simulations bear directly on V1, V3 and V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors prove two asymptotic phases (success and random guessing) for weak-to-strong training of overparameterized MNI linear classifiers. Success needs enough weak labels relative to feature-spectrum parameters, even when the weak teacher is near chance. Simulations at n=50 corroborate the predicted phases, but the transitions are not sharp. They add that multilabel analysis supports using logits or soft labels for weak supervision when available.
record.recipe_differences: Uses minimum-norm interpolation of linear classifiers over stylized Gaussian features (plus a class-averaging simulation), hard pseudolabels, and test error/accuracy rather than pretrained-model fine-tuning and PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on the weak and strong feature parameters and the number of weakly labeled examples m; the paper also reports class averaging doing significantly better than MNI in non-asymptotic settings.
record.problems: The main results rely on a stylized Gaussian, bi-level and subset feature model and 1-sparse true labels. Simulations use n = 50, 8 independent weak-model trials, 16 strong-model trials per weak model, and 100 test points; plotted results are not tabulated as exact values.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results omitted. The paper's cited Burns et al. empirical results are prior-work results, not this study's own results.

untested.parts: Pretrained language models and the PGR metric; only stylized linear classifiers are studied.
Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling of weak supervisors and loss variants are not tested. Averaging vs MNI is compared without PGR.
Real model sizes, NLP/chess/reward-modelling tasks and empirical representations.
All parts. Weak imitation under a tri-level ensemble is only conjectured (Section 4); no distribution-shift or correlated-error results.
All parts; no vision or other modality.

missing.what: Remark 3.4: with identical weak and strong parameters, τw2s=τstrong=τweak, so the strong model cannot bootstrap itself.
Class averaging does significantly better than MNI non-asymptotically, and fstrong trained on m clean labels beats both fw2s and fweak in every plot (ceiling).
The finite-sample transition is not sharp (PGR<1). The 1-sparse assumption is argued to be necessary for a sharp asymptotic transition.
Weak multilabel supervision can succeed for multiclass where the same number of clean one-hot labels would fail.

record.verdict_notes: Theory paper. Verdicts hold only within the stylized Gaussian spiked-covariance model. The simulation rows' figure captions are garbled in the extracted text: the record likely swapped strong and weak parameter tuples, and Fig 3b/3d captions may be duplicated. Check against the PDF. Burns et al. results cited in the paper are not this study's results.

versions.untested_parts: Does not evaluate pretrained language models or report PGR; tests a stylized linear-classification version using test error and accuracy.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensemble of weak supervisors, or loss-variant PGR comparison.
Does not compare real model sizes, NLP/chess/reward-modelling tasks, or empirical representations. Studies binary and multilabel classification in a parameterized feature model.

Does not test supervisor-uncheckable behavior, distribution shift, or correlated weak/strong model errors. A theoretical failure regime is reported, but it is not one of these specified failure modes.
Provides results under its stated Gaussian, overparameterized linear-model assumptions; does not establish conditions for arbitrary models or tasks.
No vision or other non-language modality is studied.

rows.size_stated: Strong feature dimension d scales as ⌊n^p⌋; model is an overparameterized linear classifier.
rows.operation_detail: Minimum ℓ2-norm interpolation on m = nu strong-feature examples with hard pseudolabels generated by fweak.

conditions.value: q + r > u; qweak + rweak > 1; u < (p + 1 + q + r − (qweak + rweak))/2
u > qweak + rweak − min{1 − r, τstrong}, with τstrong = p + 1 − 2(q + r)

rows.baseline: Weak supervisor test error is 1/2 − on(1) under the paper's desiderata.
rows.note: The theorem gives vanishing test error for the strong student in this parameter regime, while the weak model's error tends to chance.
rows.check: Link is fine. V1 holds only in a stylized linear-model sense: error goes to o(1) while the weak error is 1/2−o(1).
